title: History of Risk Assessments of the Organophosphate Pesticide Chlorpyrifos at the US Environmental Protection Agency, 1980‒2024. | History | American Journal of Public Health | EBSCO Research
description: This article analyzes the history of risk assessments of the organophosphate pesticide chlorpyrifos by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), focusing on the period after the 2000 ban on its household uses. It highlights how federally funded, place-based epidemiological studies—particularly involving children in farmworker and environmental justice communities—challenged the EPA's earlier reliance on corporate-sponsored, laboratory-based toxicology that prioritized acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition as the sole toxicity mechanism. Despite growing scientific evidence of chlorpyrifos's neurodevelopmental harms, EPA risk assessments largely marginalized these findings for two decades, influenced in part by coordinated skepticism from corporate-aligned experts and regulatory mandates balancing economic and health interests. The article concludes that EPA's epistemological preference for "de-placed" laboratory data over "place-based" epidemiology has hindered protective regulatory action, underscoring the need for reforms that better integrate diverse scientific evidence and address conflicts of interest in pesticide risk evaluation.

title: Happening Now: DEEP Deputy Commissioner Emma Cimino is joining the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), state and local partners in Stratford to mark the completion of remedy construction at… | James Fowler
description:
Happening Now: DEEP Deputy Commissioner Emma Cimino is joining the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), state and local partners in Stratford to mark the completion of remedy construction at Operable Unit 4 (the former Raybestos Memorial Ballfield).

The 14-acre parcel is part of the broader Raymark cleanup effort and represents an important milestone after more than 30 years of collaboration to address Raymark Waste, including asbestos, lead, arsenic, and PCBs.

More than 100,000 cubic yards of Raymark Waste have been consolidated and secured at OU4 under a permanent, multi-layered engineered cap designed to isolate contaminants and prevent future exposure.

The project also included important safety and community protections, along with a significantly improved stormwater conveyance system and pump station.

With the remedy now complete, this site is ready for safe commercial redevelopment and productive reuse.

Under Governor Ned Lamont's leadership, Connecticut is continuing to turn long-polluted properties into safer, healthier places that support economic development and stronger communities.

Thank you to EPA, the US Army Corps of Engineers, the Town of Stratford, Congresswoman  Rosa DeLauro, local health officials, and all partners who helped move this complex cleanup forward.
